Fear can arise in response to a threat to your life, health, or well-being, or to that of someone you care about.

## Words describing fear

Anxiety, apprehension, dread, edginess, fright, horror, hysteria, jumpiness, nervousness, overwhelm, panic, shock, tenseness, terror, uneasiness, and worry.

## Prompting events and interpretations

Events can include danger, earlier threat cues, unfamiliar situations, darkness, being alone, public performance, or possible failure. Interpretations may predict harm, rejection, embarrassment, loss, helplessness, incompetence, or inability to cope.

## Body changes, expressions, and action urges

Breathing and heart rate may change; muscles tense; the stomach may feel knotted; you may sweat, shake, feel cold, freeze, scan, seek help, hide, flee, or avoid.

## Aftereffects

Threat cues may remain vivid and the body activated. Relief after escape can reinforce future avoidance.

## When fear fits the facts

Fear fits when there is a threat to life, health, or well-being. If danger is near, protect yourself; if it is not, check the probability and available coping resources.

## Acting on the urge, Opposite Action, and Checking the Facts

When danger is real, freeze or run if needed, remove the threat, and do what gives you control. When fear does not fit, approach what is safe, take in information, use a confident posture and voice, and practise paced breathing.
